content:
Osteoporosis and arthritis are different conditions that often happen together. Arthritis affects joints and causes pain and stiffness. Osteoporosis makes bones weaker and more likely to break, and usually causes no symptoms until a bone breaks. Rheumatoid arthritis, steroid tablets, older age, the menopause and low activity all raise the risk. If you have any of these, or you have broken a bone after a minor fall, ask your GP whether you need a fracture risk check or a bone density (DEXA) scan. Keep active with strength, balance and weight-bearing exercise, get enough calcium and vitamin D, reduce your falls risk, and never stop or change a prescribed bone or arthritis medicine yourself.

This guide is for people who have arthritis and have been told they have osteoporosis or low bone density, or are worried they might, and for the family who support them. If you take steroid tablets, see bone protection on steroids as well. For a short explainer of the difference between the two conditions, see osteoporosis vs arthritis.

Osteoporosis and arthritis: what is the difference?

The names sound alike but they are different problems.

  • Arthritis affects joints. Osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis cause pain, stiffness and sometimes swelling, and you usually feel them every day.
  • Osteoporosis affects the strength of bones. The NHS explains that it develops slowly over several years and usually causes no obvious symptoms, so many people do not know they have it until a bone breaks after a minor fall or bump.

Osteoporosis does not cause joint pain by itself. But the two often happen together, and having both changes what matters most: protecting your joints and your bones, and especially avoiding falls.

Why people with arthritis can be at higher risk

The NHS lists these among the things that raise the chance of osteoporosis:

  • older age and the menopause
  • rheumatoid arthritis and some other health conditions
  • taking steroid tablets, such as prednisolone, especially for long periods or repeated courses
  • not getting much exercise, which can happen when joints are painful
  • being underweight, smoking and drinking too much alcohol
  • a parent with osteoporosis or a broken hip

Painful joints can also make you less steady on your feet, which raises the chance of a fall. A fall is what turns weak bones into a broken wrist, hip or spine.

Signs to watch for

Because osteoporosis is usually silent, the signs are often signs of a broken bone:

  • breaking a bone after a minor fall or injury, such as falling from standing height
  • sudden back pain, especially after lifting, bending or a jolt
  • getting shorter, or your spine becoming curved or your posture more hunched

These can be caused by small breaks in the bones of the spine. Do not assume new back pain is just your arthritis. See your GP if back pain is not getting better after a few weeks, or if your posture is changing.

Bone density scans and fracture risk checks

Your GP can assess your risk of breaking a bone using a fracture risk tool. NICE guidance on assessing fracture risk says this should be considered for older adults and for younger people with risk factors, such as long-term steroid use or a previous fragility fracture. Depending on the result, you may be referred for a bone density scan, also called a DEXA scan.

  • A DEXA scan uses low-dose X-rays. It is quick and painless, and you lie on your back on a couch while the scanner passes over your hips and lower back.
  • If lying flat is painful because of your arthritis, tell the scanning department before the day. They may be able to help with pillows or positioning.
  • The result is used alongside your risk factors to decide whether you need treatment.

If you have broken a bone after a minor fall, many hospitals have a fracture liaison service or bone health clinic that checks whether osteoporosis was involved. Ask your GP or the fracture clinic if this has not been offered.

Exercise that is safe for bones and joints

Exercise is good for both conditions. NICE says exercise is a core treatment for osteoarthritis, and the Royal Osteoporosis Society recommends exercise for bone health, including for people who already have osteoporosis. The kinds that help most are:

  • Muscle strengthening, such as sit-to-stands from a chair, step-ups and lifting light weights or tins. Strong muscles protect joints and help bones. See our beginner strength programme.
  • Weight-bearing activity, such as walking, if your joints allow it. Short, regular walks are better than one long one.
  • Balance practice, which lowers the chance of falling. Tai chi and the exercises in our balance training guide are good places to start.

If you have had a spinal fracture or have been told your bones are very fragile, ask a physiotherapist which movements to adapt. Many people are advised to avoid sudden, forceful bending forward while lifting, but you should not stop moving altogether. Gentle, regular activity is safer than rest.

Calcium, vitamin D and food

Bones need calcium and vitamin D.

  • Calcium is found in milk, cheese and yoghurt, fortified plant milks, tinned fish where you eat the bones (such as sardines), green leafy vegetables, and bread made with fortified flour. The NHS advises that most people can get enough calcium from a varied diet.
  • Vitamin D comes mainly from sunlight on skin in summer. The NHS advises everyone in the UK to consider a daily vitamin D supplement in autumn and winter, and all year round if you are rarely outdoors. See our vitamin D in autumn and winter guide.
  • Only take calcium tablets if your doctor or pharmacist recommends them, and take them as they advise. They can interact with some medicines.

Eating enough overall matters too. Being underweight is a risk factor for osteoporosis, and enough protein helps keep the muscles that protect you from falls.

Bone medicines

The NHS explains that some medicines slow down bone loss (bisphosphonates, such as alendronic acid) and others help build new bone. Which is best depends on your scan results, your age and your other health conditions, and your doctor will talk through the options with you.

  • Some bone tablets must be taken in a particular way, such as first thing in the morning with water while sitting upright. If stiff hands or a painful back make this hard, tell your pharmacist. There may be another form you can take.
  • Tell your dentist if you take bone medicines, and keep up dental check-ups.
  • Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself, including steroids and arthritis medicines. If you are worried about side effects, talk to your GP, pharmacist or rheumatology team first.

Cutting your risk of a fall

Preventing falls is one of the most useful things you can do when you have weak bones and painful joints. NICE guidance on falls recommends that older people who have fallen, or are at risk, are offered a falls assessment.

  • Ask your GP about a falls clinic if you have fallen or feel unsteady.
  • Ask for a review of your medicines, especially if any make you dizzy or drowsy. See blood pressure tablets, dizziness and falls.
  • Have your eyes checked regularly, wear well-fitting shoes with a good grip, and keep floors clear and well lit.
  • Use a walking aid if it helps you feel steadier. See choosing a mobility aid.
  • If you live alone, make a plan for what to do if you fall. See our falls plan for living alone.

When to get help

  • See your GP if you think you may be at risk of osteoporosis, if back pain is not getting better after a few weeks, or if your posture is changing.
  • Ask for an urgent GP appointment or use NHS 111 if you have had a fall or injury and the pain is not getting better.
  • Call 999 or go to A&E if you have severe pain after a fall, cannot put weight on a leg, or cannot get up. Do not drive yourself.

For carers and family

  • Help the person keep active rather than doing everything for them. Strength and balance are protective.
  • Help make the home safer, such as with lighting, rails and clear floors.
  • If the person falls, do not rush to lift them if they may have broken a bone. Make them comfortable and call for help.

Common questions

Does osteoporosis cause joint pain?

Not by itself. Joint pain is usually from arthritis. Osteoporosis usually causes pain only when a bone breaks, including small breaks in the spine.

Can I still exercise with osteoporosis and arthritis?

Yes. Strength, balance and weight-bearing exercise help both. A physiotherapist can adapt exercises if you have had a fracture.

Should I ask for a bone scan?

If you have rheumatoid arthritis, take steroid tablets, have broken a bone after a minor fall or have other risk factors, ask your GP whether a fracture risk check or DEXA scan is right for you.
